newsitem.title: UGANDA: Disease hits Uganda coffee, experts urge action.
newsitem.headline: Disease hits Uganda coffee, experts urge action.

text.p: Urgent action must be taken against a coffee disease devastating plantations in Uganda and eastern Congo, according to researchers at a scientific workshop here on Wednesday.

"From what we saw yesterday (Tuesday) during our visits to some of the affected areas, the situation is very serious and calls for an immediate response," one researcher said after a visit to areas affected by coffee wilt disease.

The disease, also known as tracheomycosis, has hit 12 growing districts and researchers fear that if it is not checked early enough, it could completely wipe out Uganda's coffee plantations in a few years.
Coffee is Uganda's main cash crop, accounting for up to 65 percent of the country's foreign exchange earnings. Some 2.5 million people are directly employed in the sector.
Julie Flood of the International Mycological Institute (IMI) told Reuters that the coffee wilt was serious enough to threaten Uganda's entire crop.
"We must try and eradicate the disease as soon as possible," she said, although she could not say how long this would take.
Flood said tracheomycosis was so destructive because it killed the whole coffee plant before spreading to another.
The first cases of coffee wilt in Uganda were in the western area of Bundibugyo in 1993 but it has since spread to central districts.

"What is causing much fear is the fact that it is spreading rapidly and its ability to cause losses to the country," said G.J. Hakiza of the Uganda Coffee Development Authority (UCDA), the industry's top policy body.
The workshop aims to formulate a regional approach to tackling tracheomycosis and will generate terms of reference for a project to be submitted to donors for funding.
